lesson.title: The Simplest Filter: Building a Low-Pass Out of One R and One C
lesson.summary: The RC low-pass filter is the concrete, buildable version of the low-pass concept, a single resistor and capacitor whose familiar RC time constant sets the cutoff frequency directly, connecting the time-domain behavior of an RC circuit to its frequency-domain response.
lesson.body:
You met the RC Circuit in the time domain: charge a capacitor through a resistor and its voltage rises, or falls, with a characteristic time constant τ = RC, reaching about 63% of its final change after one time constant. The RC low-pass filter is the same physical circuit, a resistor in series with the signal and a capacitor from the output node to ground, viewed instead in the frequency domain, the specific circuit that makes the general idea of Low-Pass Filter concrete and buildable.

The two viewpoints are not separate facts to memorize, they are the same RC time constant seen two ways. The cutoff frequency is fc = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2πτ). A large τ, meaning the capacitor charges and discharges slowly, corresponds to a low fc, heavy filtering that only lets very slow, low-frequency, changes through, exactly as you would expect: a circuit too sluggish to keep up with fast voltage swings in the time domain is, by the same token, one that attenuates fast, high-frequency, signals in the frequency domain.

Take R = 4.7 kΩ and C = 10 nF, 0.01 µF. The time constant is τ = RC = 4700 times 10 times 10 to the minus 9, which is 4.7 times 10 to the minus 5 seconds, 47 µs. The cutoff frequency is fc = 1/(2π times 4.7 times 10 to the minus 5), about 3386 Hz, roughly 3.39 kHz. As a check on the cutoff definition, at f = fc the magnitude is |H| = 1/√2, about 0.7071, or 20 log10(0.7071), about minus 3.01 dB, confirming the minus 3 dB point.

The inverse relationship between RC and fc also gives you a quick design tool: doubling either component halves the cutoff frequency. Doubling C to 20 nF while keeping R = 4.7 kΩ gives RC = 9.4 times 10 to the minus 5 seconds, and fc = 1/(2π times 9.4 times 10 to the minus 5), about 1693 Hz, which is exactly half of the original 3386 Hz, as the inverse proportionality predicts. That direct, predictable relationship between component values and cutoff frequency is what makes the RC low-pass filter the default starting point for real filter design, from smoothing a rectified power supply to setting the treble roll-off in an audio tone control.
